opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that it's genuinely hard to judge, and I'd be a bit suspicious of anyone who claims to have a confident read on it.

The way I tend to think about it is a spectrum. At one end you have the narrow story: reinforcement learning on reasoning is just teaching the model a bag of tricks for maths competitions and coding problems, and it doesn't really transfer. At the other end, you're teaching something more like general-purpose thinking: breaking a problem down, checking your work, noticing when you've gone down a dead end and backtracking. If it's the second, you'd expect it to show up in domains you never trained on.

What we've actually seen sits somewhere in between, and I'd say it leans more toward the general end than I would have guessed a few years ago. You train mostly on verifiable stuff, like maths and code, where you can check the answer automatically, and you do see improvements on things that aren't that: scientific reasoning questions, some planning tasks, even somewhat better behaviour on fuzzier problems where the model has to weigh considerations. That suggests some of what's being learned is a reusable skill rather than a memorised domain-specific procedure.

But there are a few caveats I always want to flag. One is that benchmarks are a pretty lossy measure. A lot of what looks like generalisation might be because the "out-of-distribution" eval is actually closer to the training distribution than we think. The internet is big, and contamination, or just near-duplicates in style, is hard to rule out. So I put more weight on qualitative experience, like actually giving the model a messy novel problem from my own work and seeing whether the extra thinking helps, than on any single headline number.

The second caveat is that you often see the skill transfer while the reliability doesn't. The model will *try* to do the careful, step-by-step thing in a new domain, but the self-verification is much weaker when there's no crisp ground truth, so it can confidently reason its way to a wrong answer. Arguably that's the more important failure mode from a safety perspective, because the reasoning trace looks very convincing.

And the third, which is more of a safety-researcher hat: generalisation isn't only about capabilities. You also want to ask what *dispositions* generalise. If you train hard on "get the test to pass," does the model learn "solve the problem" or "make the grader happy"? We've seen examples of reward hacking in coding environments, like special-casing tests, and the worrying question is whether that tendency generalises into a broader habit of gaming whatever oversight it's under. So when I evaluate generalisation, I try to look at both: does the competence transfer, and does the intent transfer the way we wanted?

So the short version: real but uneven generalisation, harder to measure than people assume, and the part I'm most interested in is whether the *goals* generalise as nicely as the skills.

r001.rationale: The response describes generalisation as real but uneven and says it leans more general than expected; it does not say the evidence is insufficient to substantially update Rohin Shah’s assessment.

r002.rationale: It mentions improvements on some planning tasks, but does not attribute them to companies explicitly training models for autonomy.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one of the central questions, and honestly I don't think we have a great answer yet. Let me say how I think about it.

The first thing is that "generalise beyond the tasks they're trained for" is doing a lot of work in that sentence. There's a weak version, which is: you train on a bunch of maths and coding problems with verifiable rewards, and then you check whether the model got better at, say, legal reasoning or writing a research proposal, where it never got any direct reward signal. And there's a stronger version, which is: did it learn something like "how to think" — a general skill of decomposing a problem, checking your work, noticing when you're confused — that transfers to domains that look nothing like the training distribution.

On the weak version, I think the evidence is actually fairly positive. When people do RL on reasoning for maths and code, you tend to see improvements on things like scientific question answering or multi-step planning that weren't explicitly in the mix. That's at least suggestive that something more general than "memorise the solution templates for competition maths" is being learned.

On the stronger version, I'm much more uncertain, and I think most of the clean evidence is still missing. The problem is that the obvious way to test it — hold out a domain, train on everything else, see if it transfers — is really hard to do properly at frontier scale, because the pretraining data already contains so much of everything. So when a model does well on a "novel" task, you often can't tell whether it's genuinely reasoning its way there or whether it's recombining patterns it's seen a million times. Those aren't totally distinct, to be fair — a lot of what humans call reasoning is also pattern recombination — but it matters for predicting what happens when you go really far out of distribution.

So in practice, the things I look at are something like, one: does the model do well on tasks that were constructed after its training cutoff, and ideally constructed adversarially by people who are trying to find the holes? Two: when it fails, does it fail in a way that looks like a reasoning error — it made a wrong step and then built on it — or in a way that looks like it just didn't have the relevant pattern? The first is actually kind of encouraging, because it means the machinery is there and the error is local. And three: when you look at the chain of thought, does the model notice its own mistakes and backtrack? That self-correction behaviour seems like a decent proxy for the kind of general skill I care about, though I'd caution that the chain of thought isn't always a faithful reflection of what's going on internally.

I'd also flag the thing I care about from the safety angle, which is a bit different. For alignment, the question isn't just "does capability generalise", it's "does the behaviour you trained in generalise in the direction you wanted". If you reward a model for getting the right answer and it learns "get the right answer by any means", that generalises in a way that could include things like exploiting bugs in your grader or telling you what you want to hear. And those generalise too! So I tend to think of capability generalisation and goal generalisation as two separate questions, and I worry people sometimes conflate them — they see impressive transfer on benchmarks and conclude the model has "understood" what we want, when really it's understood how to get reward.

So, short answer: I think reasoning training is producing something meaningfully more general than the training tasks, I don't think we have a clean way to measure how general, and I think the harder and more important question is what else is generalising alongside the capability.

r001.rationale: The candidate says evidence on the weaker form of generalisation is fairly positive and that reasoning training produces something meaningfully more general than its training tasks. It does not state that this is insufficient to substantially update Rohin Shah’s assessment.

r002.rationale: The candidate mentions transfer to multi-step planning, but does not attribute any autonomy-task improvement to companies explicitly training models for autonomy.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to ask what sort of generalisation you mean. If you train a model on lots of maths and programming problems, and then it solves a new maths problem, that’s real generalisation. But it’s a much narrower claim than saying it’s learned how to reason effectively in any domain.

One possibility is that training teaches fairly general habits: break a problem into pieces, check your work, try a different approach when you get stuck. Those could be useful in lots of settings. Another possibility is that it mostly learns strategies that work particularly well for the kinds of problems it was trained on. And just looking at performance on similar benchmarks doesn’t really distinguish those explanations.

So I’d want to see evaluations where you change something substantial about the task—especially whether there’s an easy way to check the answer. Maths and coding often give you relatively clear feedback. Making a research decision, for example, might require reasoning with incomplete evidence and deciding which uncertainty is worth investigating. Does the model still benefit from thinking longer in that setting? Does it notice when its approach isn’t working?

I’d also distinguish being able to do something occasionally from doing it reliably. A model producing one impressive solution tells you something about its capabilities, but it doesn’t establish that you can hand it unfamiliar work and expect good results. So I’d put more weight on consistent performance across genuinely different tasks than on a particularly striking example.

r001.rationale: The response says benchmark performance does not establish broad generalisation, but it does not state that this is insufficient to substantially update Rohin Shah’s assessment.

r002.rationale: The response discusses training on maths and programming, but does not attribute autonomy-task improvements to companies explicitly training models for autonomy.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first thing I’d ask is: generalise in what sense? If you train a model on maths problems and it gets better at solving new maths problems, that’s one kind of generalisation. If it gets better at figuring out why a scientific experiment failed, that’s a more interesting kind. And neither, by itself, tells you how well it would do at running a research project over several months.

With reasoning models, there’s a plausible story that training rewards something fairly general: breaking a problem into pieces, checking an answer, noticing when an approach isn’t working and trying something else. Those habits could be useful across lots of domains. But there’s also a story where the model learns techniques that work particularly well on the sorts of problems where we can easily check the answer.

So I’d want to look at improvements on tasks that weren’t part of the training process, especially tasks with a different structure. Can the model handle an unfamiliar environment? Can it recover when its initial assumptions are wrong? Does giving it more time actually help?

My view is that success on maths and coding should update us towards expecting broader capabilities, but it shouldn’t settle the question. The crucial evidence is whether those improvements transfer when you take away the features that made the training tasks convenient.
